**Louis Armstrong ("Satchmo")**
An enormously influential New Orleans jazz trumpeter and singer, mentored by King Oliver. With his Hot Five and Hot Seven bands he recorded "Potato Head Blues" and "Heebie Jeebies," a track that helped popularize scat singing. He is also famous for singing "What a Wonderful World" ("I see trees of green, red roses too") and "Hello, Dolly!"

**Miles Davis and Kind of Blue**
A trumpeter and bandleader whose 1959 album Kind of Blue is a landmark of modal jazz. It opens with "So What," whose famous "So What chord" stacks three fourths with a major third on top, and it also includes "Freddie Freeloader," "All Blues," and "Flamenco Sketches." Davis also released Birth of the Cool and Someday My Prince Will Come.

**Dizzy Gillespie's bent trumpet**
The bebop trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie played a trumpet with its bell bent upward and was known for his hugely puffed-out cheeks. He wrote "A Night in Tunisia" and "Salt Peanuts," and with the Cuban percussionist Chano Pozo he co-wrote "Manteca," a founding tune of Afro-Cuban jazz.

**Wynton Marsalis and Blood on the Fields**
A trumpeter who is artistic director of Jazz at Lincoln Center. His oratorio about slavery, Blood on the Fields, opens with "Calling the Indians Out" and in 1997 became the first jazz composition to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. Early in his career he played in Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers.

**"West End Blues"**
A 1928 recording by Louis Armstrong and his Hot Five that opens with a famous solo trumpet cadenza. The cadenza, which climbs to a high note, is considered one of the greatest moments in early jazz.

**Also sprach Zarathustra**
Richard Strauss's tone poem, which opens with trumpets playing the rising "nature" motif C–G–high C over a low pedal note. The opening is famous from the sunrise scene in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

**Brandenburg Concerto No. 2**
A concerto by J. S. Bach whose solo group (concertino) is trumpet, recorder, oboe, and violin. Its very high trumpet part was written for the valveless natural trumpet in the clarino register. Today it is often played on the small "piccolo" trumpet, which Maurice André popularized for Baroque works.

**Trumpet Voluntary**
The popular name for Jeremiah Clarke's Prince of Denmark's March, a stately Baroque piece often played at weddings.

**Mahler's Symphony No. 5**
This symphony opens with a solo trumpet call built on repeated C-sharps. The call launches a funeral march in C-sharp minor.

**Haydn and Hummel concertos for Anton Weidinger**
Anton Weidinger, a Viennese trumpeter, developed the keyed trumpet, which could play the full chromatic scale for the first time. Haydn wrote his Trumpet Concerto in E-flat for him, and Johann Nepomuk Hummel wrote his Trumpet Concerto in E major for him.

**Pictures at an Exhibition "Promenade"**
In Maurice Ravel's orchestration of Mussorgsky's piano suite, a solo trumpet plays the opening "Promenade" theme. The melody begins G–F–B-flat and switches between 5/4 and 6/4 time.

**Fanfare for the Common Man**
Aaron Copland's work for brass and percussion. After a percussion introduction, three trumpets play the opening melody, which rises through F, B-flat, and F.

**"The Trumpet Shall Sound"**
A bass aria from Part III of Handel's Messiah, accompanied by a prominent solo trumpet. Its text is "The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised."

**The Pines of Rome**
Ottorino Respighi's tone poem. In "Pines Near a Catacomb," an offstage trumpet plays a solo. The finale, "Pines of the Appian Way," brings in buccine (ancient Roman horns, usually played by modern brass instruments) to depict a victorious Roman army.

**Arban's method and "The Carnival of Venice"**
Jean-Baptiste Arban wrote the standard teaching method for trumpet and cornet, often called the trumpet "Bible." He also wrote famously difficult virtuoso variations on the folk tune "The Carnival of Venice."
